title: Three Notes From the Day: A Reflection That Doesn’t Require Feeling Grateful
subtitle: A brief evening exercise asks what went well—and what helped it happen. It is a way to notice details, not a demand to make every day feel good.
imageAlt: Two friends sit at a kitchen table in the evening, writing brief notes in separate notebooks beside a cup of tea.
imageConcept: A warm, unposed evening scene: two friends at a kitchen table, each making a few handwritten notes in a notebook, with everyday details—a mug, keys, a half-read book—visible nearby. The mood is thoughtful rather than celebratory.
body:
Some days offer obvious bright spots. Others are mostly errands, uncertainty or getting through what needed doing. A short reflection called “Three Good Things” is not meant to overrule the second kind of day. Its basic prompt is modest: write down three things that went well, then note why each happened. The point is not to claim that the day was good overall, or to produce a grateful feeling on demand. It is to give particular moments a little attention and consider what contributed to them.

That distinction matters. A person might record that a bus arrived in time, a colleague clarified a confusing task, or dinner was ready when they got home. None of those details makes a larger difficulty disappear. They can simply be true alongside it. The exercise is most useful when it leaves room for the whole day rather than asking a few positives to stand in for it.

In the original “three blessings” exercise, participants wrote each evening about three things that went well that day and why they went well. The routine was generally used over a week. The “why” is part of the exercise, not an optional flourish: it invites a person to notice what made the moment possible. Maybe someone offered help; maybe you made a choice that protected your time; perhaps several ordinary circumstances happened to line up.

That explanation does not need to be profound or flattering. “I got outside because my neighbor texted to ask if I wanted to walk” is enough. So is “I finished the form because I opened it before checking messages.” The note is a small account of events and contributors, not a score for how well you managed your life. The original researchers tested this and other brief exercises in a randomized online study, where the three-blessings activity was associated with better outcomes than the comparison exercise; results differed across the activities tested [1].
Why name the cause, not just the moment?

A list of pleasant things can become a hunt for highlights. Adding a reason makes the reflection more specific: it brings attention to the conditions, actions and relationships that shaped an event. “The call was good” is a starting point. “I asked my sister a question I had been avoiding, and she had time to listen” describes what made the call matter.

This isn’t a claim that every positive event is under personal control. A kind message may have arrived unexpectedly. A hard task may have gone smoothly because another person made space for it. Naming those contributors can make the note more accurate, not more self-congratulatory. It can also make ordinary moments count without requiring a milestone: a quiet lunch, a repaired misunderstanding, a task done well enough, or a moment of rest that was actually available.

There is research behind the exercise, but it does not establish a guaranteed mood benefit for every person. In a randomized trial with health-care workers, participants received prompts to complete a digital version three times a week for three weeks. Positive affect improved slightly at one month and remained significantly improved at three months; depression, gratitude and life-satisfaction scores did not differ significantly between groups [2]. That is a useful reminder that a brief practice is not a substitute for treatment or support, especially when someone is struggling.

A separate 2025 study compared a one-week version of the standard exercise with a nature-focused adaptation. Among 330 participants, the two approaches were statistically equivalent on affect balance and life satisfaction in that study [3]. That finding concerns those measured outcomes in that particular comparison; it does not show that nature is necessary, or that either version works equally well for everyone. Taken together, the studies support a modest framing: this is a structured reflection worth trying if it suits you, not a prescription or a promise.
Keep the notes small and concrete

If you want to test it, choose a time when you can pause in the evening and use a notebook, a notes app or a scrap of paper. For one week, write three things that went well that day and one plain reason for each. “Went well” can mean pleasant, useful, relieving or simply better than expected. The entries need not be impressive, and they do not need to be shared.

Try writing in the language of events rather than evaluations. Instead of “I was productive,” you might note “I sent the two emails that were holding up the project because I worked through them before lunch.” Instead of “I had a great day with my family,” record one scene and its contributor: “We ate together; my brother changed his plans so he could stay.” If a reason is unclear, say so. A blank or tentative explanation is more honest than forcing a lesson from the moment.

There is no requirement to complete all three entries every night, and stopping is a valid response if the task feels strained or unwelcome. It may not fit during acute grief, exhaustion or a period when positivity is being used to dismiss a real problem. Nobody should be asked to do it to prove they are coping, appreciative or resilient. A reflection can make space for good details without asking anyone to feel better about what hurts.

If three positive events do not come to mind, do not stretch the definition until it feels false. You could set the exercise aside. Or, as an untested adaptation, write one neutral fact about the day—what took up time, what changed, or what you noticed. That is not the research protocol, and it need not lead anywhere. It is simply another way to record a day without grading it. If low mood or distress is persistent, a journal exercise is not a replacement for reaching out to a trusted person or a qualified professional.
Leave the page with room for the whole day

For a first week, treat the notebook as a place to collect observations, not a report card. At the end, look back only if that feels useful. You might notice that certain people, choices or conditions appear in several entries; you might notice no pattern at all. Either outcome is information, not a verdict about your character or your life.

Try the exercise on an ordinary evening, not as a test after a particularly hard one. Write what went well, name what helped, and let the rest of the day remain present too. If the page starts to feel like an obligation, close it. The value of the practice lies in its invitation to pay attention—not in finishing a week, producing gratitude, or finding a silver lining where there isn’t one.
